edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, Software Architecture in Practice 4th ed., Performance tactics (Manage Resources: Introduce Concurrency)
edges.note: After parallelizing event streams onto threads, a scheduling policy must be chosen and applied via Schedule Resources.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 4th ed., Performance tactics (Maintain Multiple Copies of Computations)
edges.note: Replicated services/servers require a load balancer to assign new work among the copies.
Scale-out (replicate computations) vs scale-up (faster/more processors) are competing ways to add capacity.
Multiple computation replicas are the units run in parallel; concurrency exploits the replicas.
Scale-out designs replicate both data and computation so replicas can serve requests independently.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 4th ed., Performance tactics (Maintain Multiple Copies of Data: replication and caching)
edges.note: Data replication is one of the two named realizations (with caching) of maintaining multiple copies of data.

edges.cite: Bass et al., SAiP 4th ed., Energy-efficiency tactics (Resource Monitoring: static vs dynamic classification models)
edges.note: Two ways to estimate energy: static from cataloged specs/benchmarks vs dynamic model over transient workload.
A dynamic energy model (regression over past executions) is fed by real-time consumption data collected via metering.
Both yield per-resource energy figures: metering measures actual draw, static classification estimates from specs.
Monitoring energy via metering supplies the signal that drives when/where to reduce usage.

edges.cite: Bass et al., SAiP 4th ed., Energy-efficiency tactics (Reduce Resource Usage)
edges.note: Reduce Usage consolidates VMs onto fewer physical servers so idle machines can be powered down.
Removing wasted computation lowers energy draw, reinforcing device/consolidation-level usage reduction.
Energy-annotated discovery lets requests be routed to the most efficient provider, aiding usage reduction.
Runtime matching of requests to providers is performed against a service registry / discovery service.
Capping the processing rate is a sub-tactic of the Manage Work Requests grouping under Control Resource Demand.
Lowering sample frequency reduces the incoming work stream, a form of managing work requests.
Ordering events by importance so low-priority ones can be dropped is a work-request management sub-tactic.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 4th ed., Performance tactics (Limit Event Response; Bound Queue Sizes)
edges.note: Bounded queues define the overflow point that triggers limiting or dropping events; the two are paired.
Throttling is a concrete admission-control mechanism that caps the rate at which responses are processed.
A load-leveling buffer smooths bursts; bounding its size sets the overflow policy that protects resources.
A leveling queue decouples arrival bursts from processing, complementing SLA-based arrival control.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 4th ed., Performance tactics (Schedule Resources = priority assignment + dispatching)
edges.note: Schedule Resources consumes the priority scheme set by Prioritize Events to order dispatching.
Both trade computational accuracy/fidelity for bounded, predictable latency under resource pressure.
Both are Control-Resource-Demand tactics cutting time/work spent per event to meet latency targets.
Better algorithms plus removing indirection both lower work per event, reinforcing demand reduction.
Meet a latency goal either by optimizing the algorithm (do less work) or by adding hardware capacity.
Auto-scaling is a dynamic, demand-driven realization of adding resources at runtime.
Additional processors give the parallelism introduced by concurrency somewhere to run, compounding speedup.
Deadline/rate-monotonic scheduling depends on bounded per-event execution times to guarantee schedulability.

edges.cite: Bass, Clements & Kazman, SAiP 4th ed., Performance tactics (Prioritize Events is frequently paired with Limit Event Response)
edges.note: Under overload, a priority scheme decides which events to drop when the response rate is capped.
Concurrent processing dispatches work through queues whose sizes must be bounded to cap resource consumption.
